item: Row 310: a Python read of a store never drops the running app's locks on it
key_paths: src/database/connect.py src/backup/stream_backup.py src/database/at_rest_state.py src/monitoring/page_reading.py src/database/page_auth.py src/database/repair.py src/database/read_only_uri.py tests/test_store_locks_survive_python_reads_row310.py
summary: On Linux and macOS closing any descriptor on a file drops every fcntl lock the process holds on it, SQLite's included. is_encrypted_file (run on every connect), the encrypted backup byte copy (every restore safety copy and stream backup), the stream backup's member reads and the header/page readers opened and closed the live store, so a second process (the country migration, a CLI repair) could take and write a store a running app still had connections on; measured: the migration TOOK the store after one header read. The encrypted leg was refused only by accident (its taker read first and met the app's surviving -shm locks); a taker that set EXCLUSIVE first took it on both legs. Every such read now goes through connect.store_reader/store_file/open_held: a read-only O_CLOEXEC O_NONBLOCK descriptor on a regular file, counted in use, closed after the read only when no other descriptor of this process is on the file or its SQLite group (X, X-wal, X-shm, X-journal), no SQLite open is in flight (connect() and open_plain_read_only count themselves in under the same lock) and no other reader uses it; otherwise parked and closed by a later read once the group is free. The byte copy reads that descriptor at explicit offsets, checks it is the file at the path (no link followed) before and after, copies exactly the size read once, refuses a short read or size change and removes the partial; the destination is opened O_EXCL O_NOFOLLOW. Windows keeps its old paths. Two-process tests on both legs and both taker orders, after every Python read, a backup snapshot and an app-level migration; mutation-checked.
